newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Taiwan delegation slips in for HK handover.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan delegation slips in for HK handover.

text.p: Taiwan's delegate to ceremonies marking Hong Kong's handover to China slipped into the British colony on Sunday hoping for a "win-win-win" future for the three Chinese communities.

Koo Chen-fu, the official in charge of Taiwan's contacts with China, was optimistic that even though Beijing is its bitter rival, links between Hong Kong and his country would survive the handover unchanged.
Koo, China's least welcome guest at Monday's gala celebrations, pointed out that the majority of Taiwan's investments in China were made through Hong Kong.

"I sincerely hope existing channels for communications (between Hong Kong and Taiwan) will be kept open and a more unified, more solid, more harmonious reciprocal relationship will be built," he told reporters at Hong Kong airport.
Taiwan also has significant investments in Hong Kong itself with sizeable communities of Taiwanese spread through the colony where the Taiwanese flag has been a familiar sight.

In Taiwan on Saturday, tens of thousands of people braved rain to join a massive "Say No to China" rally, demanding their island not be swallowed up like Hong Kong but granted a United Nations seat as a new Republic of Taiwan.

The crowd, put by police at well over 70,000 -- one of the biggest in Taiwan history -- denounced communist China's long-time claim to the island, home to the defeated Chinese Nationalist government since the end of the civil war in 1949.
Taiwan political groups universally reject Beijing's offer of reunion under the "one country, two systems" model that brings Hong Kong back to China after 156 years of British rule.
Koo, chairman of the Straits Exchange Foundation which looks after negotiations with Beijing, is not a government minister unlike nearly all other countries' heads of delegation.
He is one of 60 Taiwanese invited to the ceremonies by the Hong Kong government. Under the handover arrangements, Britain, Hong Kong and China could each invite guests of their choice.
Koo said Taiwan-Hong Kong relations had steadily grown since his country split off from mainland China and the strength of the ties could help even Beijing.
"Both to the people in Hong Kong and Taiwan, as well as to the relations across the Straits (China), this (growth in ties) will prove the most beneficial and positive approach," Koo said.
"I naturally ponder a great deal about ways to promote goodwill along the three sides of the Taiwan Straits so as to create a win-win-win future," he said.
